coverage.assessment: Two setups are weakened. 'Warranted' dogmatism and 'supremely fitted by knowledge' lost their stated grounds in the revision. 'Necessarily followed Seward' has been thin since the first draft.
Times, places and Hay's arrival remain clear. In the Seward paragraph, 'he had some means' follows a Henry 'he', but 'unknown to other Senators' makes the referent clear.
Seward's line keeps its attribution and occasion ('at dinner, after Mr. Adams and he had made their speeches'). Sumner's denunciation correctly remains reported, not performed.
Dates and quantifiers are preserved. One minor loss: the 'right or wrong' hedge on secession is gone.
The revision removed two cues that separate the old narrator from the young man: 'The inevitable followed...' and 'Going over the experience again...'.
The Seward portrait loses its central paradox. Several self-deprecating ledger lines are trimmed.
The Lincoln misjudgment now ends at 'lack of apparent force' and has lost its ironic verdict. The Southern-conspirators contrast with Sumner's 'defection' is thinner.
All three dependencies have both endpoints present in the abridged texts. Chapter 018 lost its exact 'quarrel with Mr. Adams' sentence, but 'eight years of broken ties' still carries the link.

findings.claim: The revision cut two things the first draft kept. The first is the claim that Seward himself was 'too simple a nature to know' which was mask and which nature. The second is the list 'never petty or personal; his talk was large'. As a result, 'What was more unusual' now compares only to 'the youth of his sympathies'.

It also dropped 'Going over the experience again, long after all the great actors were dead, he struggled to see where he had blundered.' As a result, the paragraph explaining his obedience now begins abruptly after 'there it ended'.

strengths: All seven planned verbatim units survive intact, including the mosquito image and Seward's dinner line with its full attribution.
The Wide-Awake procession keeps its full sentence and its closing 'not that of innocence'.
The timeline is clean: Feb 23 arrival, March 4 hand-off to Hay, mid-March return to Horace Gray.
The 'would have lost' admission still frames the Lincoln portrait as the young man's misjudgment.
The vultures-of-patronage passage and the million-lives cost are preserved verbatim, giving the March verdict its weight.
summary: The revision keeps the plan's skeleton. All seven verbatim units survive, and so do the continuity checks: Lincoln's arrival on Feb 23, March 4 as the hand-off to Hay, the 'would have lost' frame, the private rupture, and the return to Horace Gray in mid-March. All three dependencies hold. The revision's own cuts fall on lines that carry voice and interpretation rather than events: Seward's self-ignorance, the retrospective 'inevitable'/'blundered' frame around the Sumner rupture, the ironic verdict on Lincoln, and the grounding for Sumner's 'warranted' dogmatism. Each can be restored with a single sentence. Nothing here is a blocker.
